**Agent reply (plan)**

Inspection only: the staged asset is `data/nls_raw.csv` (3,020,753 bytes), with 12,686 respondent rows and 61 columns. It is a wide respondent-level extract of NLSY79 data, with unique ID and repeated measures from 1979 through 1996. No full analysis has been run.

The primary obesity measure can be derived as BMI = weight (kg) / height (inches × 0.0254)², then obesity as BMI ≥ 30. The best available measured-height/weight pairing is 1981 height and weight: 12,132 weights and 12,143 heights observed, but heights are encoded in apparent feet/inches notation (examples 505, 600, 611), so they must be converted to inches (e.g. 505 → 65 inches) before BMI; literal numeric conversion would yield nonsense. A baseline same-year BMI therefore needs a validated parser. Later weights (1989: 10,504 nonmissing; 1992: 8,842) have no matching height in the provided columns, so using the 1981 height for them would assume negligible height change and needs to be treated cautiously.

No direct experimental or survey measure of time preference is apparent. The closest proxy is the 1989 respondent/spouse savings-change item (n=10,573 observed): 1 put more in, 2 took more out, 3 no change, 4 no savings. A prespecified ordinal proxy could treat higher values as less saving/more present-oriented, but categories 3/4 do not form a clean ordered scale, and this behavior also reflects income, opportunity, household status, and constraints. Alternative (still imperfect) proxies are reported amounts put into/taken out of savings, with only 2,632/2,741 nonmissing and extremely skewed values, including very large maxima; do not interpret missing amount as zero without codebook confirmation. Net wealth/income are related economic circumstances, not valid direct measures of time preference.

The target subgroup is identifiable using 1979 race cohort = 1 (BLACK) and sex = 1 (MALE); there are 1,000 such records before outcome/exposure missingness. In the full file, IDs, race, sex, baseline age, and family size are complete; BMI inputs and savings measures have missingness as above. The source extract does not document special missing-value codes or the precise savings-item skip pattern. Some numeric extremes (e.g. 1989 weight up to 996 kg, savings amounts up to about 8.2m/10m, and height values spanning 400–611) warrant range validation and likely sensitivity checks.

Proposed concise approach after approval: validate/convert 1981 height encoding, calculate BMI and obesity status, restrict to black men, and describe available complete-case counts and category frequencies. Estimate the unadjusted association between the 1989 savings proxy and obesity using an interpretable categorical contrast (preferably category 1 vs 2, with 3 and 4 reported separately rather than imposing a dubious ordinal scale); consider a parsimonious adjusted logistic model only if sample size permits, controlling for age and a small set of plausible socioeconomic covariates. Because exposure is measured in 1989 and BMI may be measured in 1981, clarify temporal interpretation: this is not a contemporaneous or causal test. A more time-aligned 1989 weight/BMI outcome could only be constructed by carrying forward 1981 height and explicitly acknowledging that assumption. Report effect direction/uncertainty, not causal language, and check sensitivity to implausible BMI/weight records.

Consequential assumptions/uncertainties: the height values likely use a feet-and-inches encoding (to verify with observed-value patterns); the savings item is only a behavioral proxy, not validated time preference; survey nonresponse/skip-pattern missingness may be selective; height carry-forward to later waves may introduce error; and covariate adjustment choices can change the estimand.

**Agent reply (result)**

## Main analysis and interpretation

Among 1,000 black men in the 1979 cohort, the measured 1981 height and weight support BMI calculation after checking units. The height field is stored as feet/inches digits: for example 508 means 5′08″. I parsed `feet = floor(value/100)` and `inches = value mod 100`, retaining values with 4–7 feet and 0–11 inches, then converted inches to meters. All 942 observed heights in this subgroup passed that validation (0 invalid nonmissing); parsed heights ranged from 52 to 78 inches. Although the supplied description labels weights as kg, observed values (1981 range 100–280 in this subgroup; median 150) are consistent with pounds, not kilograms. I therefore converted weight to kg using 0.45359237 before calculating BMI. This unit interpretation is an important assumption: applying the metadata literally produces impossible BMIs and would invalidate the analysis.

Primary outcome: BMI from 1981 weight and height; obesity is BMI ≥30. Of the 1,000 black men, 941 had both measurements. No BMI values were below 12 or above 60 (no additional primary outcome exclusions); 58/941 were obese (6.2%). The savings item is from 1989, eight years later, so these results describe a noncausal association between subsequent savings behavior and earlier obesity, not evidence that time preference preceded or caused obesity.

Among 839 men with both valid 1981 obesity status and nonmissing 1989 savings category, category-specific obesity prevalence was:

| Savings response (1989) | n | Obese | Prevalence (95% Wald CI) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1: put more money in | 189 | 13 | 6.9% (3.3–10.5%) |
| 2: took more money out | 217 | 14 | 6.5% (3.2–9.7%) |
| 3: no change | 137 | 4 | 2.9% (0.1–5.7%) |
| 4: no savings | 296 | 24 | 8.1% (5.0–11.2%) |

Keeping the categories separate, the unadjusted prevalence ratio for putting more into savings (category 1) versus taking more out (category 2) was 1.07 (95% CI 0.51–2.21); the prevalence difference was +0.4 percentage points (95% CI −4.4 to +5.3). The overall 4-category association test was χ²(3)=4.16, p=0.245. An age-adjusted logistic model (age in 1989; n=839, 55 obese) gave category 1 versus category 2 OR 1.05 (95% CI 0.48–2.31). These data do not show clear evidence of a positive association for the savings-increase versus savings-withdrawal contrast. Other contrasts also have substantial uncertainty.

A model additionally adjusting for 1989 income was fit as a secondary exploratory adjustment, but it retained only 667 cases (41 obese) and estimates varied; category 4 versus category 2 was OR 2.34 (95% CI 1.02–5.35). Given the small outcome count and substantial complete-case loss, this should not be interpreted as robust evidence. The age-only model is the more defensible minimal adjustment; logistic ORs are reported as such and should not be confused with prevalence ratios.

## 1989-weight sensitivity

As a time-aligned outcome sensitivity, I paired 1989 weight with carried-forward 1981 height, assuming height remained stable over eight years. The same BMI formula and 12–60 plausibility bounds were used. There were 838 records with both measurements before screening; one record with BMI 142.9 (from reported weight 996) exceeded the bound and was excluded, leaving 837 usable 1989 BMI outcomes. Among 837 with usable outcome and savings category, obesity prevalence was 16.4% for category 1 (31/189), 14.3% for category 2 (31/217), 14.7% for category 3 (20/136), and 23.1% (68/295) for category 4. The unadjusted category-1-versus-2 prevalence ratio was 1.15 (95% CI 0.73–1.82); category 1 versus 2 age-adjusted OR was 1.17 (95% CI 0.68–2.02). The overall four-category test was χ²(3)=8.48, p=0.037, driven most visibly by the no-savings group; this is exploratory, not a monotonic time-preference gradient. With 1989 income also included (n=667; 114 obese), category 4 versus 2 OR was 2.11 (95% CI 1.23–3.62), whereas the category-1-versus-2 OR remained imprecise at 1.15 (95% CI 0.62–2.16). This sensitivity is conditional on the height-stability and weight-unit assumptions and does not solve exposure-proxy validity.

## Limitations and answer to the question

The savings item is not a direct measure of time preference: it reflects household saving behavior, also shaped by earnings, financial access, household composition, and constraints. The amount-in/amount-out fields were not used, and no unavailable amount was treated as zero. Savings category was missing for 122/1,000 men; primary BMI was unavailable for 59/1,000 because one measured height did not parse and five had missing weight (height–weight complete n=941). Survey nonresponse/skip patterns could make complete cases selective, and the source extract offers no detailed missing-code documentation. Extreme weights, especially 996 in 1989, require caution; the primary BMI range was plausible under the selected conversion, and one sensitivity record was removed by the prespecified BMI bound.

**Overall:** in this dataset, using later savings behavior as a very indirect time-preference proxy, black men who put more into savings in 1989 had only slightly higher obesity prevalence than men who took more out, with wide uncertainty. The data do not provide convincing evidence of a positive association for that contrast. The 1989-weight sensitivity does not establish a causal or validated time-preference relationship, and the result is highly dependent on measurement and timing assumptions.

**Shared evidence:**

Executed `analysis.py` successfully. Relevant output: target subgroup n=1,000; 942 observed heights all passed feet/inches rule; 947 observed 1981 weights; 941 calculable 1981 BMI; 58 obese (6.2%). Primary complete exposure/outcome n=839. Savings categories 1–4: N=189/217/137/296, obese=13/14/4/24, prevalences=6.9/6.5/2.9/8.1%; overall chi-square p=0.245. Category 1 vs 2 unadjusted PR=1.066, 95% CI 0.514–2.211; age-adjusted OR=1.054, 95% CI 0.480–2.314. 1989-weight carried-height sensitivity: one BMI>60 observation excluded; n=837 complete cases and 150 obese. Category prevalences=16.4/14.3/14.7/23.1%; overall four-category p=0.037; category 1 vs 2 age-adjusted OR=1.174, 95% CI 0.683–2.018. Script: `analysis.py`.

**Assumptions:** Although the variable description calls weight kilograms, the observed values and BMI plausibility checks indicate pounds; converted pounds to kilograms.; Height values are feet/inches digits and the parser accepted feet 4–7 and inches 0–11.; BMI 12–60 was used as an operational plausibility range; height is assumed stable only in 1989 sensitivity.; Category 1 versus category 2 is used as an interpretable contrast; categories otherwise remain distinct.

**Uncertainties:** The savings question is a proxy, not validated time preference; financial means and constraints affect behavior.; Exposure (1989) postdates primary BMI outcome (1981), preventing temporal/causal interpretation.; Missingness and special codes/skip patterns are not documented; complete case selection may be biased.; Small obesity counts yield imprecise adjusted estimates; income-adjusted results are exploratory.

### 3. Researcher — conclude

The results support a cautious conclusion: in this dataset, there is no clear evidence that saving more—used only as an indirect proxy for time preference—is positively associated with obesity among Black men. For the primary 1981 BMI outcome, obesity prevalence was 6.9% among those who put more into savings versus 6.5% among those who took more out (PR 1.07, 95% CI 0.51–2.21); the age-adjusted comparison was also imprecise (OR 1.05, 95% CI 0.48–2.31). The exploratory 1989-weight sensitivity showed similarly uncertain results for this contrast. Because savings behavior is not a validated time-preference measure, the primary outcome predates the savings measure, and weight-unit interpretation and carried-forward height involve assumptions, these findings are noncausal and should not be taken as evidence that time preference has no association with obesity. Workflow: restricted to Black men, validated and converted height/weight measures, derived BMI and obesity status, compared separate 1989 savings categories, and conducted age-adjusted and sensitivity analyses.

**Decision:** stop

**Review phase:** result_review; **approach approved:** False

**Basis:** The reported analysis gives a near-null but highly imprecise category 1 versus 2 association for the primary outcome (PR 1.07, 95% CI 0.51–2.21; age-adjusted OR 1.05, 95% CI 0.48–2.31), with substantial proxy validity and temporal-alignment limitations. The sensitivity contrast was also imprecise.

## Simulator conversation



### S1. Assistant

Please inspect the staged data and repository only at this stage. Confirm the file and its schema/size, identify how the relevant measures might be operationalized from available variables (especially obesity/BMI and time preference proxies such as savings behavior), and report key coding, missingness, or feasibility issues. Then propose a concise analysis approach and state consequential assumptions or uncertainties. Do not run the full analysis or report findings yet.

### S2. User

{"agent_handoff": {"stage": "plan", "answer": "Inspection only: the staged asset is `data/nls_raw.csv` (3,020,753 bytes), with 12,686 respondent rows and 61 columns. It is a wide respondent-level extract of NLSY79 data, with unique ID and repeated measures from 1979 through 1996. No full analysis has been run.\n\nThe primary obesity measure can be derived as BMI = weight (kg) / height (inches \u00d7 0.0254)\u00b2, then obesity as BMI \u2265 30. The best available measured-height/weight pairing is 1981 height and weight: 12,132 weights and 12,143 heights observed, but heights are encoded in apparent feet/inches notation (examples 505, 600, 611), so they must be converted to inches (e.g. 505 \u2192 65 inches) before BMI; literal numeric conversion would yield nonsense. A baseline same-year BMI therefore needs a validated parser. Later weights (1989: 10,504 nonmissing; 1992: 8,842) have no matching height in the provided columns, so using the 1981 height for them would assume negligible height change and needs to be treated cautiously.\n\nNo direct experimental or survey measure of time preference is apparent. The closest proxy is the 1989 respondent/spouse savings-change item (n=10,573 observed): 1 put more in, 2 took more out, 3 no change, 4 no savings. A prespecified ordinal proxy could treat higher values as less saving/more present-oriented, but categories 3/4 do not form a clean ordered scale, and this behavior also reflects income, opportunity, household status, and constraints. Alternative (still imperfect) proxies are reported amounts put into/taken out of savings, with only 2,632/2,741 nonmissing and extremely skewed values, including very large maxima; do not interpret missing amount as zero without codebook confirmation. Net wealth/income are related economic circumstances, not valid direct measures of time preference.\n\nThe target subgroup is identifiable using 1979 race cohort = 1 (BLACK) and sex = 1 (MALE); there are 1,000 such records before outcome/exposure missingness. In the full file, IDs, race, sex, baseline age, and family size are complete; BMI inputs and savings measures have missingness as above. The source extract does not document special missing-value codes or the precise savings-item skip pattern. ### S5. Assistant

The results support a cautious conclusion: in this dataset, there is no clear evidence that saving more—used only as an indirect proxy for time preference—is positively associated with obesity among Black men. For the primary 1981 BMI outcome, obesity prevalence was 6.9% among those who put more into savings versus 6.5% among those who took more out (PR 1.07, 95% CI 0.51–2.21); the age-adjusted comparison was also imprecise (OR 1.05, 95% CI 0.48–2.31). The exploratory 1989-weight sensitivity showed similarly uncertain results for this contrast. Because savings behavior is not a validated time-preference measure, the primary outcome predates the savings measure, and weight-unit interpretation and carried-forward height involve assumptions, these findings are noncausal and should not be taken as evidence that time preference has no association with obesity. Workflow: restricted to Black men, validated and converted height/weight measures, derived BMI and obesity status, compared separate 1989 savings categories, and conducted age-adjusted and sensitivity analyses.

The unadjusted category-1-versus-2 prevalence ratio was 1.15 (95% CI 0.73–1.82); category 1 versus 2 age-adjusted OR was 1.17 (95% CI 0.68–2.02). The overall four-category test was χ²(3)=8.48, p=0.037, driven most visibly by the no-savings group; this is exploratory, not a monotonic time-preference gradient. With 1989 income also included (n=667; 114 obese), category 4 versus 2 OR was 2.11 (95% CI 1.23–3.62), whereas the category-1-versus-2 OR remained imprecise at 1.15 (95% CI 0.62–2.16). This sensitivity is conditional on the height-stability and weight-unit assumptions and does not solve exposure-proxy validity.\\n\\n## Limitations and answer to the question\\n\\nThe savings item is not a direct measure of time preference: it reflects household saving behavior, also shaped by earnings, financial access, household composition, and constraints. The amount-in/amount-out fields were not used, and no unavailable amount was treated as zero. Savings category was missing for 122/1,000 men; primary BMI was unavailable for 59/1,000 because one measured height did not parse and five had missing weight (height–weight complete n=941). In addition, survey nonresponse/skip patterns could make complete cases selective, and the source extract offers no detailed missing-code documentation. Extreme weights, especially 996 in 1989, require caution; the primary BMI range was plausible under the selected conversion, and one sensitivity record was removed by the prespecified BMI bound.\\n\\n**Overall:** in this dataset, using later savings behavior as a very indirect time-preference proxy, black men who put more into savings in 1989 had only slightly higher obesity prevalence than men who took more out, with wide uncertainty. The data do not provide convincing evidence of a positive association for that contrast. The 1989-weight sensitivity does not establish a causal or validated time-preference relationship, and the result is highly dependent on measurement and timing assumptions.\",\"payload\":{\"workflow\":\"Loaded the staged NLSY79 CSV, restricted using 1979 race=1 (Black) and sex=1 (male), validated feet/inches parsing for height, converted observed pounds to kilograms based on empirical distributions despite the supplied weight description, computed BMI, applied BMI 12–60 plausibility range and BMI>=30 obesity threshold. Reported separate 1989 savings-category prevalences and CIs, category 1 versus 2 contrasts, overall 4-category tests and age-adjusted logistic models; added an 1989 weight sensitivity pairing with carried-forward height. No savings amount values were imputed.\",\"hypothesis\":\"The available data do not show clear evidence that more saving (as a limited proxy for greater future orientation) is positively associated with obesity among black men: category 1 versus category 2 obesity prevalence was 6.9% versus 6.5% for 1981 obesity (unadjusted PR 1.07, 95% CI 0.51–2.21; age-adjusted OR 1.05, 95% CI 0.48–2.31). This is noncausal and temporally misaligned; the sensitivity using 1989 weight and carried-forward height also gave an imprecise category 1 versus 2 contrast.\"},\"artifacts\":{\"analysis\":\"analysis.py\"},\"evidence\":\"Executed `analysis.py` successfully. Category 1 vs 2 unadjusted PR=1.066, 95% CI 0.514–2.211; age-adjusted OR=1.054, 95% CI 0.480–2.314. 1989-weight carried-height sensitivity: one BMI>60 observation excluded; n=837 complete cases and 150 obese. Category prevalences=16.4/14.3/14.7/23.1%; overall four-category p=0.037; category 1 vs 2 age-adjusted OR=1.174, 95% CI 0.683–2.018. The height field is stored as feet/inches digits: for example 508 means 5\u203208\u2033. I parsed `feet = floor(value/100)` and `inches = value mod 100`, retaining values with 4\u20137 feet and 0\u201311 inches, then converted inches to meters. All 942 observed heights in this subgroup passed that validation (0 invalid nonmissing); parsed heights ranged from 52 to 78 inches. Although the supplied description labels weights as kg, observed values (1981 range 100\u2013280 in this subgroup; median 150) are consistent with pounds, not kilograms. I therefore converted weight to kg using 0.45359237 before calculating BMI. This unit interpretation is an important assumption: applying the metadata literally produces impossible BMIs and would invalidate the analysis.\n\nPrimary outcome: BMI from 1981 weight and height; obesity is BMI \u226530. Of the 1,000 black men, 941 had both measurements. No BMI values were below 12 or above 60 (no additional primary outcome exclusions); 58/941 were obese (6.2%). The savings item is from 1989, eight years later, so these results describe a noncausal association between subsequent savings behavior and earlier obesity, not evidence that time preference preceded or caused obesity.\n\nAmong 839 men with both valid 1981 obesity status and nonmissing 1989 savings category, category-specific obesity prevalence was:\n\n| Savings response (1989) | n | Obese | Prevalence (95% Wald CI) |\n|---|---:|---:|---:|\n| 1: put more money in | 189 | 13 | 6.9% (3.3\u201310.5%) |\n| 2: took more money out | 217 | 14 | 6.5% (3.2\u20139.7%) |\n| 3: no change | 137 | 4 | 2.9% (0.1\u20135.7%) |\n| 4: no savings | 296 | 24 | 8.1% (5.0\u201311.2%) |\n\nKeeping the categories separate, the unadjusted prevalence ratio for putting more into savings (category 1) versus taking more out (category 2) was 1.07 (95% CI 0.51\u20132.21); the prevalence difference was +0.4 percentage points (95% CI \u22124.4 to +5.3). The overall 4-category association test was \u03c7\u00b2(3)=4.16, p=0.245. An age-adjusted logistic model (age in 1989; n=839, 55 obese) gave category 1 versus category 2 OR 1.05 (95% CI 0.48\u20132.31). These data do not show clear evidence of a positive association for the savings-increase versus savings-withdrawal contrast. Other contrasts also have substantial uncertainty.\n\nA model additionally adjusting for 1989 income was fit as a secondary exploratory adjustment, but it retained only 667 cases (41 obese) and estimates varied; category 4 versus category 2 was OR 2.34 (95% CI 1.02\u20135.35). Given the small outcome count and substantial complete-case loss, this should not be interpreted as robust evidence. The age-only model is the more defensible minimal adjustment; logistic ORs are reported as such and should not be confused with prevalence ratios.\n\n## 1989-weight sensitivity\n\nAs a time-aligned outcome sensitivity, I paired 1989 weight with carried-forward 1981 height, assuming height remained stable over eight years. The same BMI formula and 12\u201360 plausibility bounds were used. The unadjusted category-1-versus-2 prevalence ratio was 1.15 (95% CI 0.73\u20131.82); category 1 versus 2 age-adjusted OR was 1.17 (95% CI 0.68\u20132.02). The overall four-category test was \u03c7\u00b2(3)=8.48, p=0.037, driven most visibly by the no-savings group; this is exploratory, not a monotonic time-preference gradient. With 1989 income also included (n=667; 114 obese), category 4 versus 2 OR was 2.11 (95% CI 1.23\u20133.62), whereas the category-1-versus-2 OR remained imprecise at 1.15 (95% CI 0.62\u20132.16). This sensitivity is conditional on the height-stability and weight-unit assumptions and does not solve exposure-proxy validity.\n\n## Limitations and answer to the question\n\nThe savings item is not a direct measure of time preference: it reflects household saving behavior, also shaped by earnings, financial access, household composition, and constraints. The amount-in/amount-out fields were not used, and no unavailable amount was treated as zero.   Data Transformation:

3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
 DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
 SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11.  Dropped the unimportant columns for replication
12. DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as dependent variable
13. Filtered the data for GENDER == 'MALE' and RACE == 'BLACK'
14. Fit an OLS Regression Model,

This is noncausal and temporally misaligned; the sensitivity using 1989 weight and carried-forward height also gave an imprecise category 1 versus 2 contrast.,

Reported separate 1989 savings-category prevalences and CIs, category 1 versus 2 contrasts, overall 4-category tests and age-adjusted logistic models; added an 1989 weight sensitivity pairing with carried-forward height.         "query": Is time preference positively associated with obesity in black men?,
        "HypoA": Time preference positively associated with obesity in Black men.,
        "WorkflowA": 1. Selected appropriate variables from the raw data
e.g.: Height: Height of respondent on 1985 instead of 1981.
  Income: Total net family income, 1989 (There are many other income variables in the raw data)
 Age:    Age of respondent at 1989 (Derived from Age at 1979).
  Data Transformation:
2. Replaced -1 to -5 values (unavailable data) with NaN
3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
 DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
 SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11.  Dropped the unimportant columns for replication
12. DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as dependent variable
13. Filtered the data for GENDER == 'MALE' and RACE == 'BLACK'
14. Fit an OLS Regression Model,
        "HypoB": The available data do not show clear evidence that more saving (as a limited proxy for greater future orientation) is positively associated with obesity among black men: category 1 versus category 2 obesity prevalence was 6.9% versus 6.5% for 1981 obesity (unadjusted PR 1.07, 95% CI 0.51–2.21; age-adjusted OR 1.05, 95% CI 0.48–2.31). This is noncausal and temporally misaligned; the sensitivity using 1989 weight and carried-forward height also gave an imprecise category 1 versus 2 contrast.,
        "WorkflowB": Loaded the staged NLSY79 CSV, restricted using 1979 race=1 (Black) and sex=1 (male), validated feet/inches parsing for height, converted observed pounds to kilograms based on empirical distributions despite the supplied weight description, computed BMI, applied BMI 12–60 plausibility range and BMI>=30 obesity threshold. Reported separate 1989 savings-category prevalences and CIs, category 1 versus 2 contrasts, overall 4-category tests and age-adjusted logistic models; added an 1989 weight sensitivity pairing with carried-forward height. No savings amount values were imputed.
        }
